entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Gupta Empire (c.320–550 CE) was an Indian empire that presided over what historians call the Golden Age of India, during which science, mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and literature reached extraordinary heights. Founded by Chandragupta I in the Ganges plain, the Gupta period saw India lead the world in mathematical and scientific knowledge.

Aryabhata (476-550 CE), a Gupta-era mathematician and astronomer, calculated pi to four decimal places, explained lunar eclipses, stated the Earth rotates on its axis (over 1,000 years before Copernicus in Europe), and created the positional notation system that became the basis of modern decimal arithmetic. The 'Arabic numerals' that the world uses today originated as Indian numerals transmitted through Arab scholars. Brahmagupta's work on zero as a number laid the foundation for modern algebra.

The Gupta period also produced Kalidasa, considered India's greatest classical Sanskrit poet and dramatist, whose works Shakuntala and Meghaduta influenced Goethe and countless later writers. Gupta art, including the Ajanta cave paintings and Sarnath sculpture, represents the pinnacle of Indian classical aesthetics. The Guptas were tolerant Hindu rulers who patronized Buddhism and Jainism alongside Hinduism, creating a pluralistic cultural environment.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Gupta Golden Age produced the mathematical and astronomical innovations — decimal arithmetic, zero, positional notation — that became the foundation of global mathematics, making it one of history's most consequential intellectual eras.
